name: Charles Young Buffalo Soldiers National Monument
author: author-C-2026-10-17
summary:
On a farm outside Wilberforce, Ohio, stands Youngsholm, the two-story brick house that Charles Young — soldier, diplomat and civil rights leader — called home. Built around 1854 in a simplified Italianate style, it was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1974, and on March 25, 2013, a presidential proclamation made the house and its adjoining farmland the 401st unit of the national park system. [1] The monument covers 59.656 acres of the original 79.14-acre farm that Charles Young acquired in two parcels in 1907; today fields, woodland and a farm pond surround the house. [2]

Young was born to enslaved parents in Kentucky in 1864, graduated from West Point in 1889 as only the third African American to do so, and served with the Buffalo Soldiers of the 9th and 10th Cavalry. He became the first African American acting superintendent of a national park, at Sequoia and General Grant in 1903, the first military attaché to Haiti and the Dominican Republic, and, by the eve of World War I, the highest-ranking African American officer in the Army and the first to reach colonel. [1] The park’s brochure describes him overcoming stifling inequality in the face of racism and oppression. The monument tells his story together with that of the Buffalo Soldiers, the Black regiments Congress created in 1866. [3]

black.html: At West Point, which Young entered in 1884 as the ninth African American cadet, the park brochure says he faced constant racial insults and social isolation from cadets and instructors; his first posting, at Fort Robinson, was marked by isolation and hostility. [3] The 2014 foundation document notes no other African American graduated from West Point until 1936, and ties his medical retirement in July 1917 to the prejudices and political pressures, under which the War Department generally kept African Americans from leading Black regiments bound for France. He rode 500 miles on horseback from Wilberforce to Washington to prove his fitness; the decision was not reversed. He died in Lagos, Nigeria, on January 8, 1922, while serving as military attaché to Liberia, and in 1923 became the fourth soldier honored with a funeral service at Arlington Amphitheater. [1] The brochure adds that his body came home at the urging of his wife and other notable African Americans. [3]

slavery.html: Young was born on March 12, 1864, near Mays Lick, Kentucky, to Gabriel and Arminta Young, both enslaved; shortly afterward Gabriel escaped slavery to fight in the U.S. Army. [2] The brochure says he joined the 5th Regiment, U.S. Colored Heavy Artillery, in Ohio in February 1865, and that after the war the family moved to Ripley, Ohio, where Charles studied under the African American abolitionist John Parker. [3] Laura Smith, a formerly enslaved woman, settled in Greene County with William Smith, a Mississippi plantation owner, who on July 14, 1858, filed manumission papers for her and their seven children; later that month she bought the house and 79.71 acres. She died in 1871, and the land stayed in her name until her heirs sold it. The Youngs’ two 1907 purchases effectively restored the boundaries of her farm, and local history holds that they may have been drawn by its connection to Smith and the Underground Railroad. [2]

women.html: While Charles served abroad, the 2019 cultural landscapes inventory says, his wife Ada oversaw the daily management of the household and farm, and around 1914 she directed construction of a bungalow on the property; in a 1914 letter from Liberia Charles discussed with his mother, Arminta, sending funds, hiring help and planning a new kitchen. Ada, who also taught at Wilberforce University, lived at Youngsholm until her death in 1953. After Charles died she sold the house and land in 1925 to family friend Claudia Harreld for $7,500, the appraisal, while the family went on living there. Struggling, she wrote in 1939 that pennies had been awfully scarce; in 1951 Harreld sold Youngsholm back to her for “$1 and other valuable consideration.” Their daughter Marie later taught French and music at Wilberforce. [2]

indigenous.html: The Park Service’s 2019 Buffalo Soldiers study says the name is thought to have arisen because, reportedly, Plains Indians compared the soldiers’ hair to a buffalo’s fur, while other sources credit their courage in combat, and more research is needed. As agents of the U.S. military, the study says, the Buffalo Soldiers facilitated westward expansion and carried out the army’s policies to “kill, subjugate, and displace native people,” though military records show infrequent instances in which they were enlisted to keep settlers off tribal lands. In the early national parks, Army soldiers restricted American Indians from using resources and holding ceremonies within parks, many of which had been their traditional homelands, and soldiers assigned to the parks enforced restrictions keeping them from returning; the study calls for that role to be explored. [4]
